items.text: The Dow closed up about 1.1%, more than 500 points, Thursday as investors moved money out of tech stocks and into Treasury bonds.
items.detail: The S&P 500 rose 0.3% and the Nasdaq 0.1% after recovering from an intraday drop of more than 1%; the S&P tech sector fell 0.5%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 5.09%, its biggest one-day drop since Aug. 1, the Wall Street Journal reported. Nike, Home Depot and Sherwin-Williams led the Dow. The moves followed the hotter-than-expected wholesale price report and Wednesday's worst day since July for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.
items.why: Money left AI-linked stocks for bonds and consumer companies as investors weighed what hotter inflation means for interest rates.

items.text: Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, seat of the internationally recognized government, was hit by Houthi missiles, killing at least two people.
items.detail: Officials first said two security personnel were killed when ballistic missiles struck al-Maashiq Palace; Yemen's health minister later put the toll at five dead and 16 injured. The information minister told the BBC the prime minister and other ministers were not hurt. Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea said the group struck what it called the Saudi military's operations headquarters in Aden. Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthi escalation.
items.why: The Houthi fight with Saudi Arabia has reached a direct strike on the Yemeni government's seat.

items.text: Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's ousted leader, had a not-guilty plea entered for him in New York federal court on new torture-conspiracy charges.
items.detail: Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were arraigned on a superseding indictment filed last week charging them with conspiracy to commit torture. Maduro called the charges false before Judge Alvin Hellerstein cut him off and entered the plea; Flores pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors say the couple ran a violent system of repression under which thousands of Venezuelans, including U.S. citizens, were killed, harassed or tortured. The new count adds to earlier narco-terrorism, cocaine-trafficking and weapons charges. The couple were captured in a U.S. military raid in January; trial is set for June 2027.
items.why: A former foreign head of state now faces torture charges in a U.S. courtroom.
items.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

items.text: The International Energy Agency's members agreed to speed up release of their remaining 100 million barrels of emergency oil, including over 20 million barrels of diesel.
items.detail: The IEA Governing Board said about 330 million barrels have been released so far under the March 2026 collective action responding to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Members agreed to accelerate the remaining roughly 100 million barrels, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to go out as soon as possible, bringing total releases above the original 400 million barrels. The board cited continued tight oil markets, especially for diesel, and urged producers to raise output.
items.why: Diesel led September's price spike, and this is the main coordinated effort to add supply.

items.text: Iraq's International Development Bank and two Iranian offshore banks were sanctioned by Treasury for allegedly giving Iran access to U.S. dollars.
items.detail: The designations, under Operation Economic Outcast and Executive Order 13902, also cover Iranian offshore banks Jazireh International Bank and Chabahar International Bank Overseas, Dubai-based oil intermediary Sayyed Ruhollah Razavi and two of his companies, Hong Kong's Elitesphere Trading, and four Iranian exchange houses and their owners. The State Department separately designated Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio for serving Iran's Karafarin Bank. Their U.S. assets are blocked, and foreign banks dealing with them risk secondary sanctions. Treasury's FinCEN also issued an alert asking banks to flag possible Iranian abuse of religious charities.
items.why: It is the latest round in Washington's campaign to cut off Iran's remaining financial lifelines during the war.
items.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury (press release)

items.text: Two chemical tankers off Romania's Black Sea coast were hit by drones, Romania's president said, and seven of one ship's 12 crew were still missing as of Friday.
items.detail: The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was struck early Thursday about a mile outside Romanian territorial waters. Five of its 12 crew were rescued, but strong winds and rough seas hampered the search for the rest, which resumed Friday with a Black Hawk helicopter placing four rescuers aboard. The Comoros-flagged Yara J was hit inside Romanian waters late Wednesday; its crew were unharmed and it was towed to Constanta. President Nicușor Dan said both ships were struck by drones, and a NATO military source said the drones came from Russia. Both were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea and is a key export route for Ukraine.
items.why: Drone strikes on tankers off a NATO member's coast have left seven sailors missing.

items.text: Ohio's EdChoice private-school voucher program is unconstitutional, a state appeals court ruled, though vouchers continue while the state appeals.
items.detail: A three-judge panel of the Tenth District Court of Appeals ruled 3-0 in Columbus City School District v. State of Ohio, upholding a Franklin County trial court that found EdChoice funds a separate school system in conflict with the Ohio Constitution. The court kept enforcement on hold pending an expected appeal. About 180,000 students use EdChoice, which became universal in 2023. Attorney General Andy Wilson said the state will appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court and that there is no immediate impact on families.
items.why: One of the country's largest voucher programs now heads to the Ohio Supreme Court.
items.court: Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals
items.source: Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals (decision)

items.text: Wholesale prices jumped 1.3% in September, the biggest monthly rise since March 2022, while retail sales rose 0.8% on pricier gas.
items.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said its final-demand Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September after 0.5% in August, and is up 6.3% over 12 months, the most since December 2022. Goods prices rose 2.6%, the largest increase since the series began in 2009; energy rose 10.8% and gasoline 20.3%. Services rose 0.8%. Separately, the Census Bureau's advance estimate put September retail sales at $745.0 billion, up 0.8% from August and 6.3% from a year earlier; August was revised up to 1.3%. Gas station sales rose 6.4% for the month, and sales excluding gas stations rose just 0.2%.
items.why: A day after 3.7% consumer inflation, the fastest wholesale price gains since 2022 point to more price pressure ahead.
items.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics (PPI release); Census Bureau (retail sales)
